name: Marco Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does your working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43, teach five beginner trumpet pupils, play paid parades with a brass band and record short horn parts for a studio. I left school after secondary classes and still ask a senior player to check a difficult score.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes a day good, and what makes it hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A pupil getting a clean first phrase is a good day. My partner drives a school bus, and with two children and a mortgage, a late studio call can upend who collects them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the brass band AI Plateau tidies a few booking emails, while the children still need us to hear a cracked note in the room. I would keep my Thursday beginner trumpet lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have four months of expenses saved, and my partner’s school-bus driving hours are steady. The mortgage still matters, but one lost horn overdub would not send us to relatives for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the five pupils and the two parade dates already paid for next month. I’d confirm the studio’s overdub fee by email this week before my partner rearranges pickup for our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work and income in that world. I can stand one cancelled studio afternoon without touching the mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a moved studio session still pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio once moved a session at short notice and paid the cancellation fee. I would check the terms again, because a promised fee is not cash in our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far do you trust the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI now and then to sort dates, but I do not ask it to judge a pupil’s breath. A tidy calendar does not teach anyone when to lift the trumpet.

say: I’d tell the band **live brass** and Thursday lessons still need people in the room.
I would use shorter **booking messages** without treating a promise as paid income.
think: Four months of **savings** and steady bus-driver hours cover one missed overdub.
I use AI for **dates**, not to judge a young player’s breathing.
do: Keep five **trumpet pupils** and two confirmed parade dates next month.
Confirm the **studio fee** by email before changing school pickup.
feel: I feel **calm** about a cancelled afternoon while our mortgage stays covered.
fieldNote: His **four-month cushion** and partner’s steady driving income make a single studio cancellation manageable this month.
He uses AI **occasionally** for dates but checks music by listening.
S0.quote: A tidy calendar does not teach anyone when to lift the trumpet.

steps.text: Keep five beginner trumpet pupils and two paid parade dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band Steady Disruption could cut the simple horn overdubs and booking calls before live parade work changes. I would ask the studio which sessions still have a player fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those horn stabs fill a useful part of my pay, and I am still learning the hard passages. The studio may keep its best player for live jobs and make the short recording parts with software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio this month for next term’s paid session list. If two overdubs disappear, I’d have the band leader show me how to check a generated horn chart for impossible breaths on an approved sample, then add a second beginner lesson only if the centre has a room and four paying families cover my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the studio work. Four months saved gives me room to test one change, but a shrinking pay list would still reach our mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the chart-checking really new for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have used AI to sort dates, not to check a horn chart. The band leader would need to show me a chart we have permission to use, and I would try it before involving pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a second lesson pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four paid families would cover the centre room and my evening at the current rate. I would not call a full room a success if the teacher went home unpaid.

say: I’d warn that simple **horn overdubs** may shrink before live parade work does.
I would ask the studio for a written **player fee** on each remaining session.
think: Short horn parts supply a **meaningful share** of my pay and may move to software.
My junior **playing skill** makes me less secure than the best player.
do: Ask the **studio** this month for next term’s paid overdub list.
Learn **chart checking** from the band leader on permitted material if two overdubs disappear.
Add a second **beginner lesson** after two lost overdubs only with an open room and four paid families covering time.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a smaller studio pay list despite four months saved.
fieldNote: His existing AI use is for **dates**; checking generated horn charts is a new supervised skill.
Extra **lessons** need a room, four paid families and coverage of his time.
S1.quote: I would not call a full room a success if the teacher went home unpaid.

steps.text: Ask studio for written next-term paid overdub list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band AGI by 2028 could do the booking, simple arranging and recorded horn parts cheaply. Robots that can do hands-on playing as well as people would follow around 2031, so the parades are on a later clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the studio to stop buying my short overdubs in 2028. Four months saved and my partner’s bus pay give us a little space, but that is a sizeable loss of my own earnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio now for written dates and the event hall whether it has a posted paid stage-crew opening. If overdubs stop in the first year after 2028, I’d apply only if the posted rate covers travel, lost lesson hours and pickup costs; I’d keep my pupils until a written offer arrives and ask the lender about temporary terms only if our reserve drops below one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing a sizeable recording income, even though I have a few months to act. The studio phone could stop before a robot ever lifts a horn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the event hall work be usable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The event hall’s work would have to be paid, not a trial shift for exposure. I would ask for the rate and hours before arranging after-school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a mortgage change quickly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the lender’s total interest cost with my partner before signing a payment change. A smaller bill next month could make the mortgage dearer later.

say: I’d tell players **recorded parts** face 2028 AGI before capable stage robots around 2031.
I would ask about a posted **paid crew role**, not assume the hall is hiring.
think: I expect my short **overdubs** to end, taking a sizeable part of my pay.
Four months of **savings** and bus wages buy time, not a permanent replacement.
do: Get written **studio dates** and check for a posted paid event-hall opening now.
Apply after 2028 only if overdubs stop and **crew pay** covers travel, lost lessons and pickup; keep pupils until offered.
Ask the **lender** about temporary terms only if savings fall below one month; check total interest before signing.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing a sizeable recording income, despite some savings.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 recorded work** from hands-on robot performance around 2031.
A crew move needs a **posted paid opening** and net pay after travel and lost lessons; lender help has a reserve trigger.
S2.quote: The studio phone could stop before a robot ever lifts a horn.

steps.text: Get written studio dates and check posted paid event-hall opening now
Apply for crew role if overdubs stop and written pay covers travel lost lessons and pickup
Ask lender about temporary terms if reserve falls below one month; check total interest

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band AGI by 2031 gives us five years to make sure our paid work is real. Capable robots for hands-on playing would follow around 2034, so even parade work needs a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become a more reliable beginner teacher by then, but I am not ready to coach advanced brass. A short course might help only if someone pays for it and I do not miss the lessons that cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the senior brass teacher this winter to watch one pupil lesson and show me what to fix. If the centre funds a short teaching course that falls outside paid hours and my partner can do pickup, I’d attend. Next term I’d add a second group only if four paying families and a centre room cover my time; in the first year after 2031 I’d keep it only while those conditions hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about future recording fees, but I can use five years without gambling our savings. I would rather practise one clear improvement than promise the children a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the senior teacher add?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The senior teacher has taught beginners for years and can tell when I rush a breath. I would ask for one observation, not claim I know everything from a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the group survive after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A second group needs four paying families at our current fee and a room the centre actually grants. I would stop the beginner trumpet group instead of spending our mortgage reserve.

say: I’d tell the band **2031 AGI** leaves time to improve teaching before capable robots arrive around 2034.
I would keep paid **parade work** while clients still book it.
think: A better **beginner lesson** could replace some recording hours if families pay.
I cannot use **mortgage money** for an unfunded course or lost teaching hours.
do: Ask the **senior teacher** to observe a lesson; take a course only if centre funds it outside paid hours with pickup covered.
Add a second **group** next term only with a room and four paying families covering my time.
Keep the **group** after 2031 only while room and four paid families cover my time.
feel: I feel **anxious** about recording fees, but have time to improve without borrowing.
fieldNote: His **steady adaptation** depends on an experienced teacher showing a useful technique first.
A course needs **funding**, no lost paid time and partner pickup; the group needs a room and four paid families.
S3.quote: I would stop the beginner trumpet group instead of spending our mortgage reserve.

steps.text: Ask senior brass teacher to observe one beginner lesson
Take centre-funded course only outside paid hours with partner pickup covered
Add second group next term only with room and four paid families covering time
Keep group after 2031 only with room and four paid families covering time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the band AGI by 2036 gives us ten years to improve our paid teaching, with capable robots for hands-on playing around 2039. I would still ask for next weekend’s parade fee in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might have more pupils and fewer studio calls, but I cannot know which parents will book that far out. Our bus wages and four months saved make the mortgage manageable now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep five pupils and paid parade dates this year, then test a second group only if four families pay for the room and my time. I’d save twenty from each paid studio session above the four-month reserve after the mortgage clears. In the first year after 2036, I’d keep that group only if four paying families still cover room and time; if they do not, I’d seek a posted paid centre assistant opening at a rate covering travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the longer future, not about our next mortgage payment. A ten-year view lets me check demand without buying a new trumpet on credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the twenty go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The twenty would go into a separate account after the mortgage is paid. I would count only the studio money already in the bank, not promised dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children may choose music or the bus depot or something neither of us knows yet. I would teach them to ask who pays and whether the work is steady.

say: I’d tell the band a **decade** lets us improve paid lessons before 2036 thinking AGI.
I would still get **parade fees** in writing before robots arrive around 2039.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and bus wages make the mortgage manageable today.
More **pupils** at 53 depend on parents actually booking lessons.
do: Keep five **pupils** and paid parades; test a second group only if four families pay for room and time.
Save **twenty** from paid studio fees above the four-month reserve after mortgage payments.
Keep the **group** after 2036 only while four paid families cover costs; seek a posted paid role otherwise.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later music work while current household bills remain covered.
fieldNote: His **savings transfer** adds to the existing four-month reserve only after a paid studio fee arrives.
The future **assistant role** needs a posted opening and rate covering travel; no job is assumed.
S4.quote: A ten-year view lets me check demand without buying a new trumpet on credit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the short horn parts could stop before I replace those fees. A real paid crew opening, written studio dates and clear lender terms would give us time to adjust.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask why I still play the easy parts slowly at home. I am still learning. The audience deserves an honest note even when the recording can be cleaned up later.

headlineQuote: The audience deserves an honest note even when the recording can be cleaned up later.
portrait: At **43**, Marco teaches beginner trumpet, plays parades and records short horn parts after secondary school.
His typical **pay**, partner’s bus work and four-month reserve keep near-term mortgage payments secure.
He uses AI **sometimes** for dates and would learn chart checking only on permitted material with a senior player.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens simple recordings first; paid crew openings and real fees guide his response.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end short studio horn parts before he replaces their fees.
whatWouldHelp: Written **studio dates**, a posted paid crew role and clear mortgage terms would help.
